title: ARRAY, STRUCT & UNNEST
description: BigQuery can store lists and nested records inside a single column. Learn to build them, read them and flatten them back into rows.

exercises.title: Build a list with ARRAY_AGG
context: An **ARRAY** is an ordered list of values in one cell. `ARRAY_AGG` is an aggregate function that collects values into an array — one array per group:
ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT x ORDER BY x)
`DISTINCT` removes duplicates and `ORDER BY` sorts the elements. (Tip: ARRAY_AGG fails if it meets a NULL — add `IGNORE NULLS` if the column can be empty.)
instructions: For each product `category`, list the departments that sell it.
Return `category` and `departments` — an array of distinct department names, sorted alphabetically.
solution: ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT department IGNORE NULLS ORDER BY department) AS departments
hints: The element order matters for the check, so keep the ORDER BY inside ARRAY_AGG.

requiredPatterns.message: Use ARRAY_AGG to build the list of departments.

exercises.title: Measure an array with ARRAY_LENGTH
context: Once you have an array, `ARRAY_LENGTH(arr)` tells you how many elements it has. This lets you filter on "how many different things" without a second GROUP BY.
instructions: Find the categories that are sold in **both** departments.
Build the department array per category in a CTE, then keep the categories where the array has exactly 2 elements.
solution: ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT department IGNORE NULLS) AS departments

requiredPatterns.message: Use ARRAY_LENGTH on the array of departments.

exercises.title: A complete calendar: GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY + UNNEST
context: `UNNEST(array)` turns an array into rows — one row per element — and can be used in `FROM` like a table.
`GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(start, end)` creates an array with every date in a range. Together they make a calendar:
FROM UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(DATE '2023-12-01', DATE '2023-12-31')) AS calendar_date
Left-joining sales onto a calendar shows days **without** sales as 0 instead of leaving them out — important for charts and averages.
instructions: The CTE `clothing_sets_sales` has one row per sold item in the small category `'Clothing Sets'`.
Build a calendar for December 2023 and left join the sales onto it.
Return `sale_date` and `items_sold` (0 on days without sales) for all 31 days, sorted by date.
hints: Use a LEFT JOIN so days without sales are kept. COUNT(s.sale_date) counts only matched rows, so empty days get 0.

requiredPatterns.message: Turn the date array into rows with UNNEST.

exercises.title: STRUCT: keep values together
context: A **STRUCT** groups several fields into one value — like a mini row: `STRUCT(name, retail_price)`. You read fields with a dot: `my_struct.name`.
Combined with `ARRAY_AGG` you get a handy alternative to `QUALIFY` for "the top row per group":
ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(a, b) ORDER BY b LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)]
That builds a one-element array of the best row, and `[OFFSET(0)]` takes the first element (arrays are 0-indexed with OFFSET).
instructions: For each `category`, find the **cheapest** product by `retail_price`. If two products have the same price, take the one whose name comes first alphabetically.
Use `ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(…) ORDER BY … LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)]` in a subquery or CTE.
hints: ORDER BY retail_price, name — ascending gives the cheapest first.
OFFSET(0) is the first element. Read the fields with cheapest.name and cheapest.retail_price.

requiredPatterns.message: Use ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(…) ORDER BY … LIMIT 1) for this one.
Wrap the columns in STRUCT(…) inside ARRAY_AGG.

exercises.title: Basket analysis: categories per order
context: Arrays are great for "basket" questions: collect what's in each order into an array, then analyse the arrays.
This is a two-step aggregation — first per order, then over the orders — which a CTE makes easy to follow.
instructions: CTE `baskets`: one row per `order_id` with `categories` = the array of **distinct** product categories in that order (all statuses).
Then count orders by basket size: return `num_categories` (the array length) and `num_orders`, sorted by `num_categories`.
solution: ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT p.category IGNORE NULLS) AS categories

requiredPatterns.message: Collect the categories per order with ARRAY_AGG.
Use ARRAY_LENGTH to get the basket size.

exercises.title: A lookup table from an ARRAY of STRUCTs
context: You can write an array of structs directly in the query and `UNNEST` it into a small table — handy for lookup tables and price bands that don't exist in the database:
SELECT * FROM UNNEST([
STRUCT('A' AS label, 0 AS low),
STRUCT('B' AS label, 10 AS low)
Joining with a range condition (`>=` and `<`) instead of `=` puts each product in the right band.
instructions: The CTE `price_bands` defines three bands: Budget (0–25), Mid (25–75) and Premium (75 and up). A product belongs to a band when `retail_price >= min_price AND retail_price < max_price`.
Join `products` to the bands and return, per `band`: `num_products` and `avg_price` (rounded to 2 decimals).
starter: STRUCT('Budget' AS band, 0.0 AS min_price, 25.0 AS max_price),
STRUCT('Mid' AS band, 25.0 AS min_price, 75.0 AS max_price),
STRUCT('Premium' AS band, 75.0 AS min_price, 1000000.0 AS max_price)
solution: STRUCT('Budget' AS band, 0.0 AS min_price, 25.0 AS max_price),
STRUCT('Mid' AS band, 25.0 AS min_price, 75.0 AS max_price),
STRUCT('Premium' AS band, 75.0 AS min_price, 1000000.0 AS max_price)
hints: FROM UNNEST([ … ]) turns the array of structs into rows; SELECT * expands the struct fields into columns.
Use >= for the lower bound and < for the upper bound so no product lands in two bands.

requiredPatterns.message: Turn the array of structs into rows with UNNEST.

exercises.title: Searching inside arrays: IN UNNEST
context: `value IN UNNEST(array)` checks whether an array contains a value — it returns TRUE or FALSE.
Combined with `COUNTIF` it answers questions like "how many sessions included a purchase?" in a single pass.
The `events` table is the largest in the dataset — this query scans more data than the others (still well within the free tier).
instructions: CTE `sessions`: group `events` by `session_id` **and** `traffic_source`, and collect `event_types` = the array of `event_type` values.
Per `traffic_source`, return `num_sessions` and `conversion_pct` = the share of sessions that contain a `'purchase'` event, in percent, rounded to 2 decimals.
solution: ROUND(COUNTIF('purchase' IN UNNEST(event_types)) / COUNT(*) * 100, 2) AS conversion_pct

requiredPatterns.message: Use IN UNNEST(event_types) to check for a purchase.
